indigenous-nations-cultures-and-communit.title: Indigenous Nations, Cultures, and Communities
indigenous-nations-cultures-and-communit.essential: How can comparing particular nations challenge stereotypes about Indigenous North America?
paragraphs: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy brought distinct nations together in a political alliance, while Pueblo communities of the Southwest developed other institutions and practices. Neither example stands for all Indigenous peoples. Before colonization, North America contained many languages, governments, spiritual traditions, and trade networks.

To compare nations responsibly, start with names and places. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy has a long history of diplomacy and collective political relationships among its member nations. Pueblo peoples, by contrast, include multiple communities with different languages and histories across the Southwest. Their forms of settlement, farming and governance developed in particular environments. Comparing these societies can reveal sophisticated approaches to cooperation without claiming that one nation represents all others.

A strong comparison uses the same questions for each case: who participated in decision making, how was knowledge shared, what resources mattered, and how do community voices describe the past? A map may show the distance between homelands, but it cannot explain why a council reached a decision. A museum collection may contain a useful object, but the object needs provenance and interpretation. Modern Native nations are authoritative participants in telling their own histories.
indigenous-nations-cultures-and-communit.task: Compare two nation-specific records and identify one meaningful similarity and one difference.
options: One example describes every Indigenous nation.
Communities varied across regions and periods.
A single image can prove all pre-contact customs.

land-resources-and-systems-of-governance.title: Land, Resources, and Systems of Governance
land-resources-and-systems-of-governance.essential: How did communities make decisions about resources and responsibilities?
paragraphs: Indigenous nations organized relationships to land and resources through systems of knowledge, responsibility, and governance. Some agricultural communities built irrigation or food-storage systems, while other nations used seasonal patterns for fishing, farming, hunting, or exchange.

Imagine a long summer drought. A council must decide how to use a shared river, stored crops and fishing areas. A fair historical investigation cannot begin by inventing a rule and attributing it to an actual Indigenous nation. Instead, compare the fictional choice with documented examples of decision-making, land stewardship and agricultural knowledge in particular communities. In many places, people balanced immediate needs with responsibilities to relatives, neighbors and future generations.

Geography influenced available resources, but did not determine one inevitable political outcome. Communities negotiated relationships, traded, built irrigation works in some regions and managed seasonal harvesting in others. To investigate a real example, ask whether the source comes from a Native community, an archaeologist or a colonial observer. Each may answer different questions, and colonial accounts may misunderstand or exclude Indigenous explanations.
land-resources-and-systems-of-governance.task: Decide how a fictional community might share a limited resource, then compare your reasoning with nation-specific evidence.
options: Environment entirely determined one universal Native government.
Political decisions and environmental knowledge interacted in diverse ways.
No community had rules for shared resources.

why-did-europeans-cross-the-atlantic.title: Why Did Europeans Cross the Atlantic?
why-did-europeans-cross-the-atlantic.essential: How can economic, political, and religious motives explain Atlantic exploration?
paragraphs: In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, European rulers and merchants sought profitable trade, power, and new routes to goods in Asia and Africa. Navigational techniques, ships, and maritime knowledge developed through exchanges across cultures, enabling longer voyages.

European Atlantic voyages expanded within networks of knowledge and commerce that were already connected to African and Asian markets. Merchants sought desirable goods, governments competed for influence, and religious ambitions shaped decisions. Maritime navigation drew on techniques and knowledge exchanged among many cultures. A navigator's route, a royal charter and a merchant's account illuminate different motives. The word exploration should not imply the lands reached were unknown to those who already lived there.

A useful decision activity places students in a fictional royal council. One adviser prioritizes direct access to trade, another seeks political prestige, and a third raises financial and human costs. Compare their arguments with actual historical evidence rather than assuming economic motives explain everything. European expeditions had consequences for Indigenous societies, and any historical judgment about voyages should identify both who benefited and who experienced harm.
why-did-europeans-cross-the-atlantic.task: Rank several possible motives using the viewpoint of a royal sponsor, sailor, and Indigenous community.
options: Columbus discovered a continent without people.
European voyages occurred in a world of existing societies and competing interests.
All travelers had exactly the same motive.

first-encounters-and-competing-perspecti.title: First Encounters and Competing Perspectives
first-encounters-and-competing-perspecti.essential: How can different accounts of first encounters tell conflicting stories?
paragraphs: When European arrivals met Indigenous communities, each side interpreted unfamiliar people and practices through its own experiences. Some encounters involved exchange and diplomacy; others included coercion, misunderstanding, violence, and resistance.

Consider a meeting reported in a European travel narrative. The writer might describe hospitality, gifts or unfamiliar customs, yet omit the negotiations and concerns of the people receiving the visitors. The account may have been prepared for a king, investor or religious audience. Its intended readers could influence what the author emphasized. A historian should distinguish what the text claims from what can be corroborated.

Archaeology, linguistic evidence, Native oral traditions and community scholarship may provide perspectives that survive outside European written records. The absence of a surviving Indigenous text does not mean Indigenous people lacked history or political agency. Learners should compare what two sources can establish about a particular place and encounter, then write a cautious explanation that identifies uncertainty instead of producing a fictional quotation.
first-encounters-and-competing-perspecti.task: Compare what a sponsor, Indigenous leader, and sailor could each emphasize about the same meeting.
options: One European journal explains everyone's experience.
Different sources reveal interests and omissions that must be investigated.
The first encounter always had a peaceful outcome.

the-columbian-exchange-and-its-consequen.title: The Columbian Exchange and Its Consequences
the-columbian-exchange-and-its-consequen.essential: What changed when living things, ideas, and diseases crossed the Atlantic?
paragraphs: After 1492, sustained contact connected plants, animals, pathogens, and peoples across the Atlantic. American crops such as maize and potatoes spread to other continents; horses, cattle, and other organisms moved into the Americas.

After sustained Atlantic contact, crops, animals, microorganisms and people moved across oceans in new patterns. Maize and potatoes eventually became important foods in parts of Africa, Europe and Asia. Horses, cattle and other introduced animals changed environments and economies in the Americas. The resulting transformations did not occur at the same pace everywhere. A careful cause-and-effect map should name a product, direction of movement, location and documented consequence.

Introduced diseases devastated many Indigenous populations, although effects varied by place and circumstance and were compounded by conquest, displacement and forced labor. The transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans was another major and violent part of these connections. The term exchange can sound equal or voluntary, but the historical processes involved dramatic differences in power. The best conclusion addresses benefits, harm, adaptation and unequal consequences.
the-columbian-exchange-and-its-consequen.task: Sort examples by direction of movement and consider who gained, who suffered, and what evidence supports each claim.
options: The exchange affected everyone equally and positively.
Movement transformed diets and environments while causing severe unequal harms.
Disease had no role in the consequences.

life-in-the-thirteen-colonies.title: Life in the Thirteen Colonies
life-in-the-thirteen-colonies.essential: How did geography and power shape daily life in Britain's mainland colonies?
paragraphs: The thirteen British colonies developed different economies and communities along the Atlantic coast. Chesapeake tobacco production relied increasingly on enslaved African labor, while New England had many towns, farms, and maritime businesses.

Daily life in Britain's mainland colonies varied by location, wealth, gender, legal status, religion and freedom. New England towns combined agriculture, maritime commerce and local institutions; Chesapeake plantations exported tobacco; and cities such as Philadelphia connected diverse communities through trade. These are broad regional patterns, not rules describing every resident. Consider a port ledger, a town record and a farm inventory. Each reveals part of the economy but not the entire experience of the people who sustained it.

Women, indentured servants, enslaved Africans, free workers and Indigenous neighbors encountered very different opportunities and constraints. Colonial settlement continued on Native homelands, with lasting consequences for land and sovereignty. In the colony comparison activity, learners should identify two concrete differences, one similarity and one person whose perspective is missing from the available source.
life-in-the-thirteen-colonies.task: Compare two colonial regions using economic activity, geography, and whose labor sustained them.
options: Every colony had an identical economy.
Regional differences coexisted with colonial hierarchies and forced labor.
Everyone in colonial society held equal rights.

colonial-economies-labor-and-enslavement.title: Colonial Economies, Labor, and Enslavement
colonial-economies-labor-and-enslavement.essential: How did labor systems create wealth and inequality in colonial America?
paragraphs: Plantation economies in the Chesapeake and the Lower South produced crops for Atlantic markets. Enslaved Africans and African Americans supplied labor through coercion, with laws increasingly making slavery hereditary and racialized.

Atlantic commercial networks created profits for merchants and landowners, while labor conditions differed sharply. Some workers earned wages, some served under contracts for a term, and enslaved people were held through coercion and laws that increasingly defined slavery as hereditary and racialized. These systems were not interchangeable. A plantation inventory may list people as property because of the enslaver's legal viewpoint, but that document must never erase their humanity.

When examining a historical ledger, distinguish the economic benefit claimed by an owner from the experience of those compelled to work. Ask what the ledger records, what it excludes and whether other sources preserve the voices or resistance of enslaved people. The activity should not require learners to role-play an enslaved person's suffering or to calculate a person's monetary value as entertainment. Instead, investigate power, exploitation and the limits of the surviving records.
colonial-economies-labor-and-enslavement.task: Examine a hypothetical ledger and annotate which costs and human experiences it hides.
options: Enslavement was an ordinary paid employment contract.
Chattel slavery was coercive and often hereditary, distinct from indentured labor.
Colonial wealth was shared equally among workers.

religion-identity-and-colonial-society.title: Religion, Identity, and Colonial Society
religion-identity-and-colonial-society.essential: How did religious beliefs shape both opportunity and exclusion?
paragraphs: Colonial communities included varied Protestant denominations, Catholics, Jews, Indigenous faith traditions, and African religious practices. Some colonies imposed established churches and limited religious freedom, while others allowed broader forms of worship.

Religious affiliation shaped laws, education, settlement and public life in several colonies, but policy changed across time and place. Some governments supported established churches and restricted dissenting groups. Others experimented with broader toleration, though rights were rarely universal. Maryland's 1649 Act Concerning Religion offered limited protections to certain Christians and was not an unrestricted guarantee of religious freedom for everyone.

A tolerance tribunal can compare actual rules without pretending all groups enjoyed equal protections. Students should evaluate who could worship publicly, who could hold office and whose beliefs were excluded. Historical claims should distinguish the stated ideals of a law from its effects in practice. The perspectives of Catholics, Protestants, Jews, Indigenous peoples, Africans and people without political influence help reveal the limits of colonial toleration.
religion-identity-and-colonial-society.task: Review a simplified historical policy and identify whom it protected and whom it excluded.
options: Colonial religious freedom was universal.
Rules could protect some groups while excluding others.
Religion had no influence on colonial politics.

colonial-maryland-and-the-chesapeake.title: Colonial Maryland and the Chesapeake
colonial-maryland-and-the-chesapeake.essential: What makes Maryland's colonial history both local and Atlantic?
paragraphs: English Maryland was founded as a proprietary colony in 1634, but the region was already home to Indigenous peoples including the Piscataway. Settlement and land expansion transformed relationships, power, and access to resources.

The English colony of Maryland began in 1634, but the Chesapeake was already home to established Indigenous communities, including Piscataway peoples. Waterways connected settlements, fishing areas, trade routes and agricultural land. English proprietors promoted tobacco production and negotiated, challenged or violated relationships with Native communities. As settlers expanded their land claims, displacement and conflict reshaped the region.

To investigate local history, use a map, a colonial record and a source representing Piscataway history or present-day community perspectives. Consider how geography influenced trade while laws and power influenced who controlled land and labor. Maryland was part of a larger Atlantic world in which tobacco, people and capital moved over long distances. A strong explanation connects those connections to specific consequences for Chesapeake residents.
colonial-maryland-and-the-chesapeake.task: Trace a tobacco shipment and identify whose labor, land, and decisions made the trade possible.
options: Maryland began on empty land.
Colonial settlement involved already-inhabited homelands and unequal power.
Tobacco played no part in Maryland's economy.

competing-empires-in-north-america.title: Competing Empires in North America
competing-empires-in-north-america.essential: Why did rival empires and Native nations contest North America?
paragraphs: Britain, France, and Spain sought influence, trade, and territory in North America. Their maps and claims often ignored the political authority and homelands of Indigenous nations.

By the eighteenth century, British and French imperial claims overlapped across parts of North America. Rivers and trading routes mattered because they connected settlements, Native nations and European commercial networks. Imperial maps sometimes colored large territories as if rulers controlled them completely, but Indigenous nations governed their own communities and pursued their own diplomatic goals.

An alliance map should identify who made a treaty or agreement, when, and under what circumstances. Native leaders might cooperate with one European power for strategic reasons while also maintaining independent priorities. Alliances changed as threats and opportunities changed. Students should avoid the simplistic idea that Indigenous peoples were merely attached to one European side; instead, compare evidence about trade, territory and sovereignty.
competing-empires-in-north-america.task: Read an imperial claim map and compare it with evidence of Indigenous political power.
options: European maps proved complete control of mapped land.
Maps often recorded claims rather than the authority people exercised locally.
Indigenous nations had no role in diplomacy.

the-french-and-indian-war.title: The French and Indian War
the-french-and-indian-war.essential: How did a regional struggle become part of a global war?
paragraphs: The French and Indian War began in North America in 1754 amid competing claims in the Ohio Valley and became part of the wider Seven Years' War. British and French forces fought alongside Indigenous allies whose strategic priorities differed.

The French and Indian War began in 1754 amid conflict over the Ohio Valley, involving British and French forces and multiple Indigenous nations with distinct interests. The conflict became part of a wider global war. British victory in 1763 transformed imperial control, yet it did not mean Native nations had surrendered their own rights or political authority.

A campaign map shows routes, forts and battles, but it cannot reveal all the diplomatic choices behind the fighting. Compare the location of Fort Necessity with the regional trade and land conflicts, then examine how the 1763 settlement changed British finances and colonial policy. The war contributed to new taxation disputes, while Indigenous resistance and border conflicts continued. Historians distinguish the war's immediate outcome from its longer-term consequences.
the-french-and-indian-war.task: Place the war's major turning points on a timeline and explain why 1763 did not resolve every conflict.
options: The war affected only European soldiers.
Indigenous nations shaped strategy and faced lasting consequences.
The 1763 treaty ended every conflict in the region.

taxes-representation-and-colonial-protes.title: Taxes, Representation, and Colonial Protest
taxes-representation-and-colonial-protes.essential: Why did new British policies provoke colonial resistance?
paragraphs: After 1763, Britain sought revenue and tighter imperial administration. The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed certain printed materials, and later policies increased disputes over Parliament's authority.

Following the costly Seven Years' War, British officials sought revenue and greater control over imperial commerce. Colonists protested laws such as the Stamp Act and Townshend duties, arguing about consent and representation. Protest methods included petitions, boycotts, public demonstrations and sometimes intimidation or violence. Not every colonial resident agreed with the same tactics or supported independence.

In a tax policy council, evaluate a parliamentary explanation, a colonial petition and the interests of people who lacked political representation. A slogan such as no taxation without representation is evidence of a political claim, not proof that its supporters sought equal voting rights for everyone. Ask how imperial debt, parliamentary authority, local assemblies and competing definitions of rights produced a constitutional conflict.
taxes-representation-and-colonial-protes.task: Choose a tax-response strategy and justify it from different historical positions.
options: All colonists agreed on independence in 1765.
Colonists debated policy while facing unequal representation at home.
The Stamp Act was passed after independence.

why-did-the-colonies-declare-independenc.title: Why Did the Colonies Declare Independence?
why-did-the-colonies-declare-independenc.essential: How did a political dispute become a declaration of separation?
paragraphs: Conflict escalated after years of disputes over taxation, representation, parliamentary power, and British military action. Fighting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775, more than a year before independence was declared.

Independence grew from years of disputes over imperial authority, military conflict and competing political ideas. The Declaration of Independence, adopted on July 4, 1776, listed grievances against George III and stated principles about rights and government. The document is both a major political argument and a historical source written for a particular purpose and audience.

Compare the Declaration's language about equality with the realities of enslavement, limited voting rights and Indigenous land conflicts. Its authors did not speak for all people in the colonies, and many residents remained loyal to Britain or sought other outcomes. An evidence board can separate complaints about specific policies from general principles, then ask how those ideas were applied, challenged and expanded across later history.
why-did-the-colonies-declare-independenc.task: Match a grievance to a constitutional idea and ask who was excluded from its promises.
options: Independence was declared before fighting began.
The Declaration followed escalating conflict and advanced contested ideals.
The Declaration immediately ended slavery.

turning-points-of-the-revolutionary-war.title: Turning Points of the Revolutionary War
turning-points-of-the-revolutionary-war.essential: Which developments changed the war's prospects and why?
paragraphs: The American Revolution included battles, diplomacy, logistics, and civilian hardship. Victories at Trenton and Princeton in late 1776 and early 1777 helped restore morale, while the American victory at Saratoga in 1777 strengthened prospects for a French alliance.

The Revolutionary War did not follow a simple path from defeat to victory. The American victory at Saratoga in 1777 helped convince France to form an alliance with the United States in 1778. The campaign in the South involved difficult fighting and choices by many communities. In 1781, French and American forces helped compel a British surrender at Yorktown, but negotiations and other military operations continued.

When ranking turning points, state a criterion before choosing a winner: military effect, diplomatic significance, public morale or longer-term consequences. A battle map may show troop movements without explaining how financing, disease, supplies or alliances shaped the result. Different criteria can support different defensible rankings. The final explanation should cite evidence rather than assume the largest battle was automatically most important.
turning-points-of-the-revolutionary-war.task: Rank Saratoga, the French alliance, and Yorktown by the kind of change each produced.
options: Yorktown was the peace treaty signed in 1783.
Saratoga, foreign support, and Yorktown affected the war in different ways.
France never supported the Americans.

patriots-loyalists-women-and-black-ameri.title: Patriots, Loyalists, Women, and Black Americans
patriots-loyalists-women-and-black-ameri.essential: How did different people experience a revolution about liberty?
paragraphs: Not all colonists supported independence. Patriots sought separation, Loyalists remained attached to the Crown, and many others made decisions shaped by family, religion, survival, and local circumstances.

The Revolutionary era divided families and communities. Patriots favored separation from Britain, Loyalists opposed it, and many people made difficult choices based on local conditions. Women contributed through labor, commerce, political writing and organizing, even while most lacked formal political rights. Free and enslaved Black people pursued freedom and security in different ways, including service connected to British and American forces.

An ethical perspective roundtable does not ask students to pretend to be enslaved individuals or to invent traumatic testimony. Instead, analyze documented choices and constraints. Compare a Patriot argument, a Loyalist concern and evidence about Black and women's experiences, then explain why one label cannot capture an entire person's circumstances. Identify whose political opportunities expanded and whose remained restricted.
patriots-loyalists-women-and-black-ameri.task: Compare three historical positions, identifying each person's risks and constraints without treating one as typical of all.
options: Every resident supported the Patriot cause.
Political commitments and survival strategies differed widely.
Black Americans played no role in the conflict.

did-the-revolution-deliver-liberty-for-e.title: Did the Revolution Deliver Liberty for Everyone?
did-the-revolution-deliver-liberty-for-e.essential: How did revolutionary ideals contrast with people's lived rights?
paragraphs: The Declaration announced an ideal of equality, but slavery continued, women remained excluded from voting in most states, and Indigenous sovereignty was challenged by expanding settlement.

The language of liberty and natural rights became central to the Revolutionary period, but independence did not immediately create equal rights for everyone. Slavery remained entrenched in much of the new nation, many women lacked the vote, and Indigenous nations confronted continued encroachment on their sovereignty and homelands. Some northern states began gradual emancipation, while other restrictions persisted.

An evidence-based liberty audit should specify the group, the right, the place and the time. Avoid turning the question into a simple yes-or-no judgment. The Revolution changed political institutions and created powerful arguments about rights, while also exposing contradictions between ideals and practice. A well-reasoned answer notes both historical change and continuing exclusion, supported by examples.
did-the-revolution-deliver-liberty-for-e.task: Compare a revolutionary promise against two concrete historical outcomes and write a qualified verdict.
options: The Declaration immediately gave equal rights to everyone.
Ideals helped inspire demands but did not eliminate exclusion.
Every state abolished slavery in 1776.

america-s-first-national-government.title: America's First National Government
america-s-first-national-government.essential: Why did the Articles of Confederation create both possibilities and problems?
paragraphs: The Articles of Confederation were adopted by Congress in 1777 and ratified in 1781. They established a union of states with a national Congress but no separate national executive or federal judicial branch comparable to those created later.

The Articles of Confederation were ratified in 1781 after being approved by Congress in 1777. They established a union in which the national Congress had limited powers. It could conduct diplomacy and request funds, but could not levy national taxes directly under the Articles. The system reflected fears of centralized authority after the Revolution.

During the 1780s, debts, interstate trade disputes and disagreements about policy exposed problems with the confederation. Yet the government also enacted important territorial policies, including the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. A confederation challenge should ask what a government could and could not do and why people disagreed about changing it. Changes in federal authority also affected Indigenous nations whose lands were claimed without their consent.
america-s-first-national-government.task: Run a simulated Congress with limited taxing power and discuss trade-offs between state autonomy and national coordination.
options: The Articles created the presidency as it exists today.
The Articles produced a weak center amid continuing disputes over authority.
The Articles gave Congress unlimited taxing powers.

debating-the-constitution.title: Debating the Constitution
debating-the-constitution.essential: How did compromise shape the Constitution, and who was excluded?
paragraphs: Delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787 to revise the national system and instead drafted a new Constitution. They argued over representation, federal power, the executive, and the relationship between states and the national government.

Delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787 to revise the nation's governing system and ultimately proposed a new Constitution. They disagreed about representation, federal authority and the balance between national and state power. The Great Compromise created a House based on population and a Senate with equal representation for states, while other compromises protected slavery and entrenched inequality.

Ratification debates continued beyond the convention. Federalists argued that the proposed Constitution could create a stronger and workable republic. Anti-Federalists raised concerns about concentrated power and the absence of explicit rights protections. A classroom convention can weigh the arguments while making clear that the original debates excluded many groups, including women, enslaved people and most Indigenous nations. Modern learners can critically evaluate a compromise without endorsing its harms.
debating-the-constitution.task: Negotiate a representation plan and write a brief argument about the consequences and exclusions of a compromise.
options: The Constitution was approved without disagreement.
Delegates compromised, but some compromises entrenched inequality.
Enslaved people gained voting rights at the convention.

the-bill-of-rights-and-individual-libert.title: The Bill of Rights and Individual Liberty
the-bill-of-rights-and-individual-libert.essential: What did the Bill of Rights protect, and whom did protections reach?
paragraphs: The first ten amendments were ratified in 1791. They recognized protections including religious exercise, speech, press, assembly, petition, and rights connected to criminal procedure and federal power.

The first ten amendments were ratified in 1791. They protect specified liberties and address powers of the federal government, including speech, religious exercise, due process and the rights of accused people. Their original legal scope differed from much of modern constitutional practice, which developed through later amendments and court decisions.

A rights-in-context activity should distinguish a constitutional principle from the outcome of a particular modern case. Students can analyze a fictional government rule and ask which amendment might be relevant, what facts are missing and why constitutional interpretation may be contested. The lesson should not suggest that everyone in the early republic enjoyed these rights equally; race, sex, legal status and political power shaped lived experience.
the-bill-of-rights-and-individual-libert.task: Match a hypothetical civic problem to an amendment and explain what else you would need to know.
options: The Bill of Rights was ratified in 1776.
The first ten amendments were ratified in 1791.
Rights were uniformly enforced for all residents in 1791.

george-washington-and-the-presidency.title: George Washington and the Presidency
george-washington-and-the-presidency.essential: How did Washington shape the responsibilities and limits of the presidency?
paragraphs: George Washington became the first president under the Constitution in 1789. His administration helped establish executive departments, set practices for consultation with advisers, and confronted economic and diplomatic challenges.

George Washington assumed the presidency in 1789 as the first president under the new Constitution. Many executive practices were not fully specified in the document, so actions taken by the first administration could become influential precedents. Washington worked with executive advisers, faced disputes about federal power and managed difficult domestic and international challenges.

An investigation of precedents might compare Washington's decision to leave office after two terms with constitutional rules enacted much later. The two-term limit became legally binding only with the Twenty-Second Amendment, ratified in 1951. Students should distinguish an influential custom from a law and evaluate how individual actions, institutions and subsequent events shape governmental practice.
george-washington-and-the-presidency.task: Distinguish a constitutional requirement from a precedent Washington established, then assess its value.
options: The Constitution originally required presidents to serve exactly two terms.
Washington established practices, including voluntary departure, that influenced successors.
Washington served as president before the Constitution was ratified.

the-emergence-of-political-parties.title: The Emergence of Political Parties
the-emergence-of-political-parties.essential: Why did political factions appear despite fears about division?
paragraphs: During the 1790s, leaders disagreed over national finance, the size and power of the federal government, constitutional interpretation, and relations with France and Britain. Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson became associated with competing political visions.

The Constitution did not establish a two-party system. In the 1790s, disputes over fiscal policy, the national bank, interpretations of federal authority and foreign relations contributed to emerging political alignments. Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson disagreed about several of these issues, although their positions and the developing coalitions cannot be reduced to one slogan.

Newspapers and pamphlets helped political leaders and readers communicate and persuade, but partisan writers could selectively emphasize evidence or attack opponents. A newspaper bias detective can compare two arguments about the same policy, identify the author's position and audience, then look for verifiable facts. A responsible analysis considers not only who appears in elite political writing but also people whose perspectives were excluded.
the-emergence-of-political-parties.task: Compare two invented editorial positions against a factual source and identify persuasive wording.
options: The 1790s parties were exactly the same as today's parties.
Early factions formed around real disagreements over policy and power.
There were no political disagreements after ratification.

challenges-facing-the-new-republic.title: Challenges Facing the New Republic
challenges-facing-the-new-republic.essential: How did the young nation test its laws, finances, and foreign policy?
paragraphs: The 1790s government faced public debt, disputes over taxation, and fears about foreign conflict. The Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania tested federal authority over an excise tax, while Washington's administration pursued neutrality during war between Britain and France.

Public debt and federal taxation tested the new government's authority. In the 1790s, opposition to an excise tax on distilled spirits developed into the Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania; Washington's administration responded by mobilizing militia forces. Supporters saw enforcement of law, while critics raised concerns about burdens and federal reach.

Foreign policy presented another dilemma when Britain and revolutionary France went to war. Washington's administration issued a neutrality proclamation in 1793, but citizens and leaders disagreed about its implications. Meanwhile, Indigenous nations defended homelands against expansion and treaties made under uneven conditions. A crisis council should identify legal authority, competing interests, short-term costs and consequences for people beyond the national leadership.
challenges-facing-the-new-republic.task: Choose among three possible government responses to a crisis and evaluate costs, legality, and whose voices were missing.
options: The early republic had no domestic or foreign challenges.
Federal authority, fiscal policy, diplomacy, and Indigenous sovereignty were contested.
The Whiskey Rebellion was a dispute about the 1776 Declaration.
